_about: Site list for harness/device-price-probe.mjs. Every URL was loaded once as mac-chrome on the date below and returned a declared price before it was admitted; the ones that did not are listed in research/device-pricing/METHOD.md §3. `visibleSelector` is the last-resort extractor and is set only where the page declares no usable price in markup; those loads are flagged `visible` in the results. No login, no Amazon.
method: 4 device profiles × 3 interleaved rounds per site, fresh incognito context per load, 3–6 s between loads; extraction json-ld → microdata → meta → visible (zeros fall through); see research/device-pricing/METHOD.md

sites.why: A hotel page with dates and occupancy in the URL on an OTA that renders a 'from USD n' rate to an anonymous visitor. No usable price in markup, so rendered text is read; the pattern anchors on 'from USD n' (desktop) / 'Final price: USD n' (phone), because the phone template lists a struck-through 'Original Price' first. In vetting the phone templates often rendered no price within 20 s headless — expect inconclusive there.

A single listing with dates in the URL; the platform is frequently named in device-pricing discussion, so it belongs on the list. Price renders only in the booking panel (desktop sidebar / phone footer) and the phone page lists 'similar listings' prices first, so the pattern anchors on '$n for 2 nights'. Rendering of the panel was intermittent in vetting (one desktop load in four showed none within 26 s) — expect inconclusive.

The one flight-search page among those tried that declares a fare in markup (JSON-LD: the lowest fare for the route/date). Fares move over minutes; the same-device control decides whether the site can be read at all.
The most-used flight metasearch; no markup price, fares are rendered client-side with an accessible label ('n US dollars'). The first labelled fare is the top result.

The only car-rental search among those tried that rendered a rate to an anonymous headless visitor (Turo: Cloudflare challenge; Sixt/Discover/Economy Bookings: no rate on the landing page). LAX, two days, sorted by price. Client-rendered list; the pattern anchors on the 2-day TOTAL because the phone template renders the per-day rate first ('$26 $52 total') while desktop renders '$52 Total for 2 days'. The first result is a sponsored slot that changed between vetting loads, so the same-device control is expected to rule this inconclusive; it is kept to show that.
Large home-goods retailer with a clean single-product JSON-LD Offer; a cheap, stable, high-volume SKU.
Largest US brick-and-mortar retailer; declares the price only in microdata (itemprop=price), which exercises the second extractor path. The page IP-geolocates a store (Ridgecrest, CA).
Electronics big-box; same SKU as the Walmart entry so the two mass retailers can be read side by side. JSON-LD Offer.

Manufacturer's own store on an enterprise platform with heavy segment-based pricing infrastructure (consumer / business / education); several configurations declared in JSON-LD, the first is the base.

A retailer with a public reputation for uniform pricing — a plausible negative control among the retailers. The page declares 24 Offers (one per iPad configuration); the first candidate in document order is a DIFFERENT configuration on the phone template than on desktop, which is the case that produced the multi-offer check (METHOD.md §1.6). The headline 'from $449' is never the first candidate.
Apparel brand store with heavy client-side personalisation infrastructure; JSON-LD lists one Offer per size.
Footwear marketplace owned by the retailer deliberately excluded from this list; a long-lived SKU with a JSON-LD Offer per size.
Direct-to-consumer luggage brand; JSON-LD Offer plus product:price meta, so two extractor paths can be cross-checked in the raw data.
A Shopify storefront — the platform behind a large share of independent retail — with a non-round sale price (135.15) that would expose rounding differences between device templates.
A single ticketed event on the largest self-serve ticketing platform; JSON-LD Offer (lowest tier). Chosen for a fixed face value rather than a resale floor.
Experience OTA; a dated-availability product with a from-price in both JSON-LD and meta. Viator, the other large experiences OTA, returned HTTP 403.
Secondary-market ticketing; declares a lowPrice per listed event in JSON-LD (24 scripts). Resale floors move fast, so this mainly tests whether a fast-moving price is correctly ruled inconclusive.

_cut_for_budget: citypass-new-york (fixed-price attraction pass, declared 149.00 USD in JSON-LD + meta on vetting) was cut to keep the run under an hour; apple-ipad already serves as the fixed-price negative control.
